Alchimia ist ein künst und ist also viell
als ein werck zu aller wolllust dieser welt, den
unterhalt ist die Sonne, das ander der Mon,
Man soll wissen das man bey den sieben Pla
neten soll erkennen sieben berge metalla bey
der Sonnen das gold beym mon das silber,
bey Jovis das zin, bey Saturnus bley, bey
Mars zinnier, bey Venus copper, bey Mer
curius quacksilber das soll man wissen
dies hier heißen geist dieser künst, welche
dem kupffer die rote brennen, und bringen
die zu silber farbe das ist das Salis Armo
niacus und Mercurius und Schwefel und A
senicum, die hier heißen geist die vormals
heißen disams als, und sind beständig.
Nu merke das fast leicht dinge sindt die sache
von zu dieser künst, aber meister sich kund woll
den wenn einem Meistern gerat, zum ersten
mall soll er können neben ein loffen die
pulver behendigkeit, zum andern soll er können
sublimiren die pulver in dem wasser, wenn
könn man die pulver der leucht in dem wasser
und konn man die pulver der leucht in
dem topfe, das sie darin rinnen, wenn
könn man die pulver brennen mit der
metallen, und man mus wissen, welcher
pulver

<column-break/>

pulver das man mus machen ist das kupffer
das auch nach seinem rechten gewicht sey, zum
dritten soll er können lassen die pulver zusammen
nach ihrer rechten sinn binden soll er können
die pulver zu dem kupffer legen behendigkeit,
zum fünfften soll er können finde machen quack
silber zu oder das bley zum fünfften das er
könne die pulver zu wasser brennen.
Also bringet man die pulver zu wasser, nun
die pulver wenn sie gefecken und gerieben, sein
kund für sie in die blasen, und fange sie
in einem wasser, so werden sie in die blasen
zu wasser, oder wie das wasser nim gewicht und
das quackalber, auch sie ball, kund verwerke das
nüun ander in ein treff, denn setze es uff ein offen,
oder in ein offen der soll dazu gemacht sein, da soll
man dem wohl mischen, und man soll das kein
ander machen, so denn es kan moglich, feuer, und
denn langer ist besser, denn für das ruin gen,
den tage, wo misse es sich untereinander, das
es sich immer geschwit in deinem haus, und wenn
man das so gemacht, so mag man das cool legen
zu dem kupffer. Und mit ein ander brennen,
so wird es gut silber.
Nu merke das zu dieser künst gehören soll man
falsch ding und meiste sach, denn sein mancher
ley pulver die heißen in dieser künst, Salarmoni
acus, Sal mason, Sal Enabrot, Salpeter, Sal nitre

ITEM IN NATALE DOMINI.

*In Die.*

*Secreta.*

<margin>R. S. Gerb. 6. Leon. 473.</margin> Oblatio tibi sit, Domine, hodiernae⁵ festivitatis accepta, qua et nostrae reconciliationis processit perfecta placatio, et divini cultus nobis est indita plenitudo⁶ Iesu Christi Domini nostri. Qui tecum vivit.

Cuius figuram Abel iustus instituit agnus quoque legalis ostendit, celebravit Abraham, Melchisedech sacerdos exhibuit, sed verus agnus, [et]⁷ aeternus pontifex, hodie natus Christus implevit. Et ideo cum angelis.

*Infra actionem.*

<margin>R. S. Gerb. 6.</margin> Communicantes et diem sacratissimum celebrantes in quo incontaminata⁸ virginitas huic mundo edidit Salvatorem Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Sed et memoriam. ℟

period the Briges, returning from Phrygia, took possession of the city and the surrounding country. They were supplanted by the Taulantii, an Illyrian tribe, who were displaced in their turn by the Liburnians, another Illyrian tribe, who were in the habit of making piratical expeditions against their neighbours with very swift ships. Hence the Romans call swift ships *Liburnians* because these were the first ones they came in conflict with. The people who had been expelled from Dyrrachium by the Liburnians procured the aid of the Corcyreans, who then ruled the sea, and drove out the Liburnians. The Corcyreans mingled their own colonists with them and thus it came to be considered a Greek port; but the Corcyreans changed its name, because they considered it unpropitious, and called it Epidamnus from the town just above it, and Thucydides gives it that name also. Nevertheless, the former name prevailed finally and it is now called Dyrrachium.

40. A portion of Pompey's forces had crossed to Dyrrachium with the consuls. Pompey led the remainder to Brundusium, where he awaited the return of the ships that had carried the others over. Here Caesar advanced against him, and he defended himself from behind the walls and dug trenches to cut off the city until his fleet came back. Then he took his departure in the early evening, leaving the bravest of his troops on the walls. These also sailed away after nightfall, with a favourable wind.

Obiciendum autem est his de natura auri quod sola secundum Hermes et in quo nulla apparet egritudo. neutra enim pars materie ipsius est imperfecta et intemperata. Cum enim sulphur lucidissimum et mundissimum per loturas fortissimas adductus ad puritatem quod nulla omnino habet unctuositate cremabilem. nec aquea humiditatem flegmatica evaporabilem: et forte in locis concavis quoque solida superficies et sepius sublimata et digestum temperato calore digeritione que pepantis vocatur. et terrea substantia que est incorporata sulphuri munda et subtilissima vaporabiliter suspensa per totam substantiam humidi radicalis ipsius sulphuris. Propter quod relinquitur quod calor illius sulphuris sit complexionals et temperamento in nullo recedens et hoc est sicut virtus masculina in composito one auri. Sicut autem argentum vivum habet duas substantias ad extrema mudificata. Tertium enim quod est in ipso calore est subiliatu non modo materialiter divisum / sed vaporaliter et subtilissimum terre forte sepius sublimatum in terre paucitatibus et vivifici caloris solis et stellarum. Sicut autem aquea subtiliati per eundem modum iterate sepius subtiliatioris / cum vitru sic insit subtiliat subtiliter. Constat quod simul mirta per calorem et dispositione loca pfocantis et reflectetis vaporem in seipsum fortissimo nexu mixtionis colligata sunt. Sulphur autem in compositionem auri non venit tantum per qualitatem sed per substantiam et cum sit subtilis substantie penetrabit ubique per argentum vivum coagulando colorat ipsum. et cum sit utrumque sublimatione ad formam superior elementorum deductum que in natura diafanitatis cum perpetuo puenit corpore habebit utrumque plenum quietatis. et cum spissentur plurime partes materie simul costabunt. hoc enim est de proprietate subtilis substantie quod constans per coagulationem plurimas partes habebit in purissimo loco. Diafanitas igitur contracta faciet colorem et trinitatem. et subtilitas facit solidationem maximam et constantia multarum partium simul in parvo loco et situ facit pondus / sicut probatur ex his que in certo mundo rationabiliter demonstrata sunt. Relinquitur autem ex solidatione et temperamento simul quod auri sit parum vaporativum vel nihil / et ideo quasi non est odoriferum. Odor autem licet non sit essentialiter fumalis evaporatio / tamen frequenter fortis odor est cum fumali evaporatione / propter quod etiam relinquit ulterius quod aurum sit incorruptibilis omni metallo et magis sustinens ignem propter fortissimam sui comixtionem in mixtura. Fumalis enim evaporatio quando dam indicat corpus corruptionem que est minus in argento et magis in ere. Et his habet causa quare aduruntur argentum quod non adurunt auri sicut sulphur et arsenica et quedam alia. Causa enim huius

Et temperantia autem auri habet quare est calidus et humidus conferens tremozi cordis et melancolie et facit tristitiam. et per virtutes atque illi que facit homine solum apud se loqui. conferunt contra auri. has passiones sive speciebus eiusdem virtutis confricatu sive etiam sumpta tritum. Et soliditate autem est quod non contingit corpora et tantum nisi difficulter. et ideo fertur in annulis et ceteris ornamentis. Et cur aurum gentium autem tingit paru / et cetera metalla tingunt multos quod continet non tangit git: ideo quia humor unctuosus in toto est ab eis separatus cui commixta est terrestre adusta in eis / et hoc stingit sicut fuligo corporis unctuosi. Multa autem puritas materie facit et rarissime invenit alij corpora post imictu / sed semper absi purum quod alii pmisser non potest retinet re tanta puritatem. et ideo generat in es. econtra rarissime invenit nisi lapidibus incorporatum. Et hoc iterum est quod invenit ut grana are nularum frequenter / quia tanta puritatem oportet esse pauca et ab illa materia elevata et quasi expulsam et ideo diversam / tamen id inventu est granum c. marchari simul. Ex his iterum constat que hec duo metalla scilicet auri et argenti assupta sunt in materia numismati a sapientibus antiquis. habent enim hoc speciale iuvamentum auri. ad hominis complexionem iuvanda et consolanda et consolanda et durabiliora et nobiliora ceteris. Purificantia autem auri sunt acita et valde sicca sicut sales et precipue sales marini et fuligo corporum unctuosorum sed sicco et later tritus. Cum autem purificari debet aurum fit testum vas ad modum cucurbite vel scutelle factum. et super illud vas fit simile illi et conglutinat in loco contactui et tenaci luto quod sapientie lutu vocat alchimia. In superiori aut sunt foramina multa que exeat vapor et fumus et postea attenuat aurum in laminas breves et tenues et ordinantur in vase. ita quod dlibet ordo laminarum subtus et supra habet pulverem fuliginis et salis et lateris farinati comixtorum et decoquit in igne forti donec purissimum est. et consumunt in eo substantie ignobiles. lutum autem sapientie de quo fiunt teite fit ex teita contrita et iterum comirta et decocta. hoc enim vas in igne positu non comminuit igne sensibili consumptione. Tamen alio modo in alchimicis sparatur lutu sapientie sed illud hic sufficiat quo aurifices utuntur. Sic igitur purificatur aurum et non excuritur in eo nisi substantie ignobiles / propter quod eleganter dicit Hermes in alchimicis suis. Cum enim sulphur lucidissimum et mundissimum per loturas fortissimas adductus ad puritatem quod nulla omnino habet unctuositate cremabilem. nec aquea humiditatem flegmatica evaporabilem: et forte in locis concavis quoque solida superficies et sepius sublimata et digestum temperato calore digerente que pepantis vocatur. et terrea substantia que est incorporata sulphuri munda et subtilissima vaporabiliter suspensa per totam substantiam humidi radicalis ipsius sulphuris. Propter quod relinquitur quod calor illius sulphuris sit complexionis et temperamento in nullo recedens et hoc est sicut virtus masculina in composito one auri. Sicut autem argentum vivum habet duas substantias ad extrema mudificata. Tertium enim quod est in ipso calore est subtiliatu non modo materialiter divisum / sed vaporaliter et subtilissimum terre forte sepius sublimatum in terre cavitatibus et vivifici caloris solis et stellarum. Sicut autem aquea subtiliati per eundem modum iterate sepius subtiliatioris / et cum vitru sic insit subtiliat subtiliter. Constat quod simul mixta per calorem et dispositione loca phocantis et reflectetis vaporem in seipsum fortissimo nexu mixtionis colligata sunt. Sulphur autem in compositionem auri non venit tantum per qualitatem sed per substantiam et cum sit subtilis substantie penetrabit ubique per argentum vivum coagulando colorat ipsum. et cum sit utrumque sublimatione ad formam superior elementorum deducta que in natura diafanitatis cum perpetuo puenit corpore habebit utrumque plenum quietatis. et cum spissentur plurime partes materie simul costabunt. hoc enim est de proprietate subtilis substantie quod constans per coagulationem plurimas partes habebit in purissimo loco. Diafanitas igitur contracta faciet colorem citrinum. et subtilitas facit solidationem maximam et constantia multarum partium simul in parvo loco et situ facit pondus / sicut probatur ex his que in certo mundo rationabiliter demonstrata sunt. Relinquitur autem ex solidatione et temperamento simul quod auri sit parum vaporativum vel nihil / et ideo quasi non est odoriferum. Odor autem licet non sit essentialiter fumalis evaporatio / tamen frequenter fortis odor est cum fumali evaporatione / propter quod etiam relinquit ulterius quod aurum sit incorruptibilius omni metallo et magis sustinet ignem propter fortissimam sui comixtionem in mixtura. Fumalis enim evaporatio quandoque indicat corpus corruptionem que est minus in argento et magis in ere. Purificantia autem auri sunt acita et valde sicca sicut sales et precipue sales marini et fuligo corporum unctuosorum sed sicco et later tritus. Tamen alio modo in alchimicis sparatur lutu sapientie sed illud hic sufficiat quo aurifices utuntur. Sic igitur purificatur aurum et non excuritur in eo nisi substantie ignobiles / propter quod eleganter dicit Hermes in alchimicis suis. XL. La virtù tiene la proprietà d'essere d'origine divina (1); conciossiacchè queste tre sue parti tutte insieme costituiscono la vera virtù; e ciascuna di esse si trova sempre colle altre due congiunta. E in effetti nella prudenza avvi ancora la fortezza, in quantochè la mente nel ricercare il vero vi si travaglia e dura fatica, nè si ristà sino a che nol ritrovi; vi è anche la temperanza, essendo che è pur cosa savia l'ignorare talune cose. Nella temperanza poi si ritrova la prudenza, che ci consiglia a non trasandare le cose utili alla vita, per non riportarne detrimento; e perciò la Medicina è di origine divina, perchè dettata da questo vero eterno: vi è anche la fortezza, acciocchè sappia egli tenersi lungi dai piaceri. Infine nella fortezza si trova pure la prudenza per difendere l'onesto; vi è poi la temperanza, acciocchè i vincitori non vogliano distruggere i vinti, che possono senza danno serbare in vita.

->*Della virtù vera.*<-

XLI. Non avvi adunque virtù alcuna che stia sola, chè ove trovi veramente la virtù, sii certo che vi si trovano tutte le altre insieme riunite: poichè le virtù, che stiano isolate, meritano appena, secondo le parole di S. Agostino, il nome di virtù (2).

(1) Cap. III.
(2) Epist. CLXVII; altrimenti XXIX ad Hieronymum, c. 3, n. 11, cap. 4, n. 14.

->*Virtutis divina origo.*<-

XL. Virtus divinae originis proprietatem obtinet (1); namque hae tres ejus partes una sunt vera virtus; et quaeque earum semper est cum aliis duabus complicata. Etenim in prudentia et fortitudo inest, ut in vero vestigando laboret, nec in eo nisi explorato acquiescat; inest et temperantia, qua quaedam ignorare sapientia est. In temperantia et prudentia inest, ne quis ad exitium usque sui utilibus vitae rebus abstineat: quare Medicinae origo divina; nam ab hoc vero aeterno dictata: inest et fortitudo, ut sustineat a voluptatibus temperare. In fortitudine et prudentia inest, ut pro honesto pugnet; inest et temperantia, qua victores nolint perdere, quos possunt servare victos.

XLI. Igitur nulla virtus solitaria, et ubi ex vero una ibi omnes Comites adsunt: solae enim virtutes vix est, ut cum Divo Augustino (2) loquar, ut nomen virtutum mereantur.

The lustre of this *bimbam* you may compare to man's knowledge, and it grows feebler and feebler as the reflection is transferred from a clear *upādhi* to one less clear, and so on till you get to the physical body. Our knowledge depends mainly on the condition of the *upādhi*, and you will also observe that, just as the image of the sun on a clear surface of water may be disturbed and rendered invisible by the motion of the water itself, so by a man's passions and emotions he may render the image of his true self disturbed and distorted in its appearance, and even make the image so indistinct as to be altogether unable to perceive its light.

You will further see that this idea of self is a delusive one. Almost every great writer on Vedāntic philosophy, as also both Buddha and Śaṅkarācārya, have distinctly alleged that it is a delusive idea. You must not suppose that these great men said that the idea of self was delusive for the same reason which led John Stuart Mill to suppose that the idea of self is manufactured from a concatenation or series of mental states. It is not a manufactured idea, as it were, not a secondary idea which has arisen from any series of mental states. It is said to be delusive, as I have been trying to explain, because the real Self is the Logos itself, and what is generally considered as the ego is but its reflection. Cum ipsi præterea credant, Heuam de corpore Adæ fuisse formatam, aiunt enim hoc voluntatis diuinæ miraculo accidisse: per eundem etiam modum respondendum eis est de Messie conceptione, ac natiuitate ex virgine. Cum diuina voluntas naturæ cursu, aut ordine minime indigeat.

CAPVT XV.
*Oppositionum recentiorum Iudæorum, matris Messie virginitatem impugnantium, confutatio.*

CAPIO.
VAMVIS hæc ita sint, Iudæi tamen nostri temporis matris Messie virginitatem impugnare cupientes, mirifico signo illo de virgineo cœptu & partu, ab Isaia dato, non desistunt, impossibile existimantes, virginem concipere, ac filium parere. Quæ afferunt hæc Isaie verba, cum dixit, *Alma concipiet & pariet filium* non de matre Messie intelligi debere, sicuti prisci eorum exposuerunt, & fides Catholica de virgine gloriosa Maria illa eadem verba prædicta fuisse, affirmat. Quocirca plura contra nos in hoc

<column-break/>

facere solent argumenta. Quibus, vt obmutescant eorum in matrem Messie latratus, te per eorum scripturas respondere cupio. Primum itaq; <margin>Primum Iudæorum argumentum.</margin> fic argumentantur. Signum hoc(inquiunt) quod propheta dedit, liberationis futuræ Regis Achaz à duobus Regibus, qui contra eum venerant, signu fuit. Christus autem vester post Achaz vltra annos quingentos, natus est. Signum igitur hoc concessionis eius ex virgine esse non potuit. GAL. Facile nobis erit huic argumento respondere, si prius <margin>Solutio.</margin> pro veritatis propheticæ intellectu, historia summatim notauerimus. Tépestate igitur qua Achaz in Iudæa regnabat, cum reges potentes duo, Syriæ scilicet & Ifrael Ierosolymæ copioso exercitu obsedissent, vt scribitur apud Isaiam 7. cap. & 4. Reg. 16. tunc misit Dominus Deus Isaiam ad Achaz, vt eum moneret, ne ab illorum Regum exercitu metueret, Ipse autem vt prauus & incredulus (etate enim idololytum cultor) prophetæ verbis credere noluit. Quam ob rem propheta eum monuit, vt ex quo ei non credebat, peteret fieri aliquod suæ liberationis signum, dicens, Pete tibi signum, vel miraculum à Domino Deo tuo. Profunda petitione & exalta eam sursum. Hoc est, Pete signum tuæ liberationis fieri, siue ex inferni profundo per alicuius mortui resuscitationem, siue de cœlo per solis stationem, sicut tempore Iehosuæ factum est. Ille autem cum impius esset, nolés à Deo signum petere, excusationem protulit, Quod hoc esset Deum tentare. Vnde ait, Non petam, & non tentabo. Cum igitur Isaias cognouisset, quod no bona fide Achaz hoc dixerat, sed potius quia Deum minime timeret, ipsum huiusmodi signo indignu iudicans signum ei dare noluit, sed illud domui Dauid dedit, dicens, Audite ergo domus Dauid, Numquid parum est vobis vexare homines, quod vexetis etiam Deum meum? Propter hoc dabit Dominus ipse vobis signum. Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium & vocabit ipsa nomen eius Emmanuel. Ex his patet, signum de virginis conceptu, & partu non fuisse datum ipsi Achaz, sed domui Dauid, ex cuius femine Messias secundum carné nasciturus erat. Negandum igitur est, quod in argumento dicitur, hoc signum scilicet ipsi Achaz fuisse datum. Ad illud autem quod dicitur, Quod cum Christus post Achaz per annos vltra quingentos natus sit, conceptio eius ex virgine eius signum liberationis prædictæ à duobus illis Regibus esse non potuit: dicimus duplex in sacra scriptura reperiri signum. Vnum prognosticum, alterum rememoratiuum. Proghosticum quidem <margin>Signum duplex pros & rememoratiuum.</margin> est respectu futuri euentus. Cuiusmodi fuit illud, quod (vt dicitur Iudicum 6. cap.) Gedeoni in vellere futuræ victoriæ indicatiuum datum fuit. Rememoratiuum vero respectu præteriti. Cuiusmodi illud extitit, quod Mosi Dominus dedit Exod. 3. ca. dicens. Hoc est, Et hoc erit tibi signum, quod miserim te. Cum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto immolabis super montem istum, gratias scilicet agens mihi de missione hac, quæ tibi imponitur. Signum igitur de virginis conceptu & partu rememoratiuum fuit, no prognosticum. Nec obstat magna temporis distantia

L'INFANTE au Page.
VA-t'en trouuer Chimene, & luy dy de ma part,
Qu'auiourd'huy pour me voir elle attend vn peu tard,
Et que mon amitié se plain de sa pareffe.

Le Page s'entre.
LEONOR.
Madame, chaque iour mefme defir vous preffe,
Et ie vous voy penfiue & trifte chaque iour,
L'informer auec foin comme va fon amour.

L'INFANTE.
I'en dois bien auoir foin, ie l'ay prefque forcée
A receuoir les coups dont fon ame eft bleffée,
Elle aime Don Rodrigue, & le tient de ma main,
Et par moy Don Rodrigue a vaincu fon deffein,
Ainfi de fes amants ayans formé les chaifnes,
Ie dois prendre intereft à la fin de leurs peines.

LEONOR.
Madame, toutefois par my leurs bons fuccez
On vous voit vn chagrin qui va iufqu'à l'excez,
Cet amour qui tous deux les comble d'allegreffe,
Fait-il de ce grand cœur la profonde trifteffe?
Et ce grand intereft que vous prenez pour eux
Vous rend il malheureufe alors qu'ils font heureux?
Mais ie vay trop auant, & deuient indifcrette.

L'INFANTE.
Ma trifteffe redouble à la tenir fecrette.
Efcoute, efcoute enfin comme i'ay combattu

XII.
Constat itaque Paracelsistarum, Weigelianorum, Mysticorum, Quakerorum & cæterorum, qui communi illuminatorum nomine vocari solent, opiniones fanaticas in eo conspirare, quod præter corpus & animam rationalem sit in homine substantialis quædam pars divinitus ipsi, &, ut plerique non dissimulant, ex ipsa divina essentia concessa. Eandem doctrinam de tribus partibus hominis satis prolixe explicat Felgenhawer im Vorhoff/ im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes: cujus fanatici libelli lectiones singulæ singularum partium rationes & Fanaticorum de iis somnia satis declarant. Conferri etiam meretur Bartholomaei Sclei anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre/ nec non das Buch des Gezeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes/ cujus Autor se ipsum vocat HIEL, das einwesige Leben GOttes/ ut & des von GOtt hocherleuchteten Matthes Weyer gründlicher Unterricht/ & similia a furiis illis conscripta librorum portenta, indigna sane quibus legendis quis bonas ac irrevocabiles horas perdat.

XIII.
Cæterum hæc de triplici hominis parte doctrina principem in ipsorum Matæologia locum obtinet. Hanc enim non modo Christianismi totius, sed omnis in universum sapientiæ, quæ in cælo & terra est, fundamentum continere ineptissime jactitat Autor des Vorhoffs Cap. XII. At vero si quem forte lateat se quinque habere sensus, vel quæ sit visus vel auditus aut reliquorum natura, anne propterea statuendum, quod isti munere suo fungi nequeant? Non equidem puto. Interim Andreas Christophorus Rafelius hoc dogma tantis extollit encomiis ut non vereatur in der Neujahrs Posaune hunc in modum de eo loqui: Das ist eigentlich der rechte Grund-Fels/ und das gewisse Fundament/ darauff das Hauß unsers Christenthums soll gesetzet/ geleget und fundiret werden/ soll es bestehen: und daraus alles predigen/ lesen/ schreiben/ GOttes Wort hören/ singen/ beten/ gute Wers

τὸ ἡμαρτημένως ἐν αὐτῇ ἐκτεθὲν ἐπανορθώσασθαι· πρότερον ἡμᾶς ἐφιστᾶν ἀξιοῖ οὗ τῷ ἐκτεθέντι τῇ προτάσεως διαγράμματι, ὅπως μὲν ἔχουσι τάξεως αὐτοῦ ἀδυνάτου προτάσεις, ὅπως δὲ αὖ τοῦ ἀναγκαίου, ἵνα καὶ θεάσασθαι δυνηθῶμεν, ὅ,τι ποτέ ἐστιν ἐν τούτῳ τὸ ἡμαρτημένως ἔχειν, διόπερ καὶ ἐπάγει ταυτί.

>> Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἀδύνατον καὶ οὐκ ἀδύνατον, τῷ ἐνδεχομένῳ, καὶ δυνατῷ, καὶ μὴ ἐνδεχομένῳ καὶ οὐ δυνατῷ, ἀκολουθοῦσι μὲν ἀποφατικῶς· αἱ περὰς μὲν γὰρ τῷ δυνατῷ εἶναι, ἡ ἀπόφασις τοῦ ἀδυνάτου ἀκολουθεῖ· ἡ οὐκ ἀδύνατον εἶναι· τῇ δὲ ἀποφάσει, ἡ κατάφασις· τῷ γὰρ οὐ δυνατῷ εἶναι, τὸ ἀδύνατον εἶναι· κατάφασις γὰρ τὸ ἀδύνατον εἶναι· τὸ δ' οὐκ ἀδύνατον εἶναι, ἀπόφασις· τὸ δ' ἀναγκαῖον πῶς ἔχει, ὅπερ οὖν φανερὸν δὲ ὅτι οὐχ οὕτως ἔχει· ἀλλ' αἱ ἐναντίαι ἕπονται· αἱ δ' ἀμφάσεις χωρεῖς· οὐ γὰρ ἐστιν ἀπόφασις τοῦ ἀναγκαῖον μὴ εἶναι, τὸ οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι· οὐδέχετου γὰρ ἀληθεύεσθαι ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἀμφοτέρας· τὸ γὰρ ἀναγκαῖον μὴ εἶναι, οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι.

Διῶν τάδε μὲν τοῦ ἀδυνάτου προτάσεις, καταφατικὰς τε, καὶ ἀποφατικὰς ἀκολούθως ἐκκεῖσθαι φυσι, καὶ ὑποτετάχθαι ταῖς τοῦ δυνατοῦ, καὶ τοῦ ἐνδεχομένου καὶ καταφατικὰς τε, καὶ ἀποφατικὰς προτάσεσι, τῇ ἀποφάσεων ἐπ' εὐθείας διαγεγραμμένων ταῖς οἰκείαις καταφάσεσι· καὶ ὅλης μὲν τῆς ἁπλῆς τοῦ ἀδυνάτου ἀποφάσεως, ὑπὸ τὰς ἁπλᾶς ἐκείνων ἀιφάσεις πεταγμένης· ὅλης δὲ τῆς ἐκ μεταθέσεως ὑπὸ τὰς ἐκ μεταθέσεως· ἀλλ' ὥσπερ φησὶν ἀντιστραμμένως τῆς ἀντιστροφῆς ποθεμόνην θεωρουμένης τὴν τῆς ποιότητος τάξιν· διότι τάδε μὲν ἐκείνων καταφάσεσιν ἕπονται αἱ τοῦ ἀδυνάτου ἀποφάσεις

༄༅། །དཔལ་ལྡན་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་རྗེ་བཙུན་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འཁོར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་གྲོལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ཡང་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གསུང་རབ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་མདོ་སྡེ་དང་རྒྱུད་སྡེ་རྣམས་ལས་ཀྱང་། མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་། འཁོར་བ་དང་ངན་སོང་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་ཐར་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །རྒྱལ་བའི་བསྟན་པ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་འཛིན་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་། བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་། སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་ནས་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

༄༅། །དེ་ལྟར་ན་སྣང་བ་འདི་དག་གི་འཁོར་ལོ་རྣམས་སོ། །ཡུལ་ལས་འཕགས་པའི་དེ་ཉིད་སྤྱན་རས་གཟིགས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་ནི། དགེ་སློང་དངོས་སུ་ཤེས་ནས་རྣམ་པར་སྤྱོད་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་མཐོང་བར་མཛད་དོ། །བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་བསྟན་པ་ནི། བསྟན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པའོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་ནི། ལེགས་པར་བརྩམས་པའི་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་སྟེ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

༄༅། །དཔལ་ལྡན་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་རྗེ་བཙུན་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འཁོར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་གྲོལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ཡང་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གསུང་རབ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་མདོ་སྡེ་དང་རྒྱུད་སྡེ་རྣམས་ལས་ཀྱང་། མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་གསུངས་སོ། །བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གསུང་རབ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་མདོ་སྡེ་དང་རྒྱུད་སྡེ་རྣམས་ལས་ཀྱང་། མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་གསུངས་སོ། །བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་བླ་མ་དམ་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གསུང་རབ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་མདོ་སྡེ་དང་རྒྱུད་སྡེ་རྣམས་ལས་ཀྱང་། མཚན་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་གསུངས་སོ། །

༄༅། །དེ་ལྟར་ན་སྣང་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་འདི་ལྟར་འཇུག་པས། ཡུལ་ལས་འཕགས་པའི་དམ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །དགེ་སློང་དངོས་གྲུབ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་དམ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །ལེགས་སོ་ལེགས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞེས་སོ། །

SCENE IX.

DORANTE, ARLEQUIN.

ARLEQUIN.
EH bien, Monsieur, mon commencement va bien, je plais déja à la foubrette.

DORANTE.
Butord que tu es.

ARLEQUIN.
Pourquoi donc, mon entrée est si gentille.

DORANTE.
Tu m'avois tant promis de laisser là tes façons de parler sottes & triviales, je t'avois donné de si bonnes instructions, je ne t'avois recommandé que d'être serieux. Va, je vois bien que je suis un étourdi de m'en être fié à toi.

ARLEQUIN.
Je ferai encore mieux dans les suites; & puisque le serieux n'est pas suffisant, je donnerai du mélancolique, je pleurerai, s'il le faut.

DORANTE.
Je ne sçais plus où j'en suis; cette avanture-ci m'étourdit : que faut-il que je fasse?

standing, build for the soul and for permanent growth but sympathy builds for nothing.

The world loves the person who will sympathize with its ailments, but those sympathetic ones have never done the world any good. Sympathy breeds into the soul self-pity and the world is filled with people who are sorry for themselves and who feel that for some unknown reason that they are having a hard time which they do not deserve. This is a false concept and those who breed it in the minds of others breed falseness.

Man must be inspired in his efforts instead of being sympathized with in his ailments. The philosopher of old never sympathized with the crying child but sought to teach him the lesson of his fall. There is seldom if ever a time when sympathy really answers the question. It is a false narcotic, which, while it eases the pain for the moment, leaves the ultimate as far off as before.

Occult students want to learn to stop sympathizing with people for into the sympathetic ears of the world are poured all its woes by individuals who live only to tell their troubles to a sympathetic listener, said listener in turn consoling them and saying how sorry he is that it is so, how sad it must be to suffer so, and so forth and on and on into nothingness. This brings into the mind of the other person the belief that they really are terribly abused, badly off, and hopelessly mistreated. This course of procedure destroys the work of the Wisdom-Religion which is seeking to prove to man that he is responsible for his own troubles and suffering and that he must labor himself for the repairing of his own temple, digging out of the debris the ruins of his own dreams. But he will never attain with the assistance of those who sympathize with him for they build in nothing but negative and willy-nilly things. The one who is truly the friend is not the one who says he is sorry and how terrible it must be but is the one who instructs and enlightens and takes the suffering of a life to show the workings of the divine powers.

There are two kinds of people in the world: one is the kind who are always bewailing, the other is the group that is eternally trying to find a real reason for the ever-changing conditions of life. The first group sympathize with everyone and everything, telling the

<column-break/>

world how sorry they are and making the rest of the world sorry too; the other group are called heartless because they have no word of sympathy to offer, and yet in their heartlessness they are humanity's truest friends. Instead of singing the emotional lullaby of the soul this second group takes the weak-kneed person who is crying for sympathy and with firmness, yet mercy and compassion, shows them the way and tells them to walk it, to forget that they are abused and march straight on to the path of light. They are the strong characters and man will never grow strong while he seeks to justify his mistakes and soothe his conscience with the sympathetic words of others. The greatest mercy in the world is to tell the truth for while it may hurt today, in eternity it brings its blessing. While today it may be harsh, tomorrow it will be appreciated. Those who spend their lives trying to justify the thing that is not as it should be and who weep with you in your infirmities go down forgotten in history's pages. The friend who raises you is the true friend; the one who weeps with you is just another fool. The more sympathy we get the more we want until all the uncertainty and unbalance of the ages rests upon our shoulders, placed there by our friends whose sympathizing kills out our own incentive to do better. Our worst enemies weep with us while our true friends weep for us as they see us nursing our meanest temperaments and greatest weaknesses with friends around to weep and wail with us.

When a great prince of Egypt died they hired mourners to weep at the tombs and great processions of white-clad figures howled and wailed behind the funeral cortege for so many pieces of silver a day. The richer the family of the departed, the more weepers were hired so that when a great dignitary died the streets literally ran with tears which were paid for at so much per. *As the moon of the fifteenth night, the heart till the age fifteen:*
*Then the brightness wanes, and the darkness comes with love.*²

*All things change, we are told, in this world of change and sorrow;*
*But love's way never changes of promising never to change.*³

यथा रूपस्याऽऽलोकस्तथा रूपज्ञानं, विकारकारणं मनसो विषयान्तरम् । यथाऽग्निः पाकस्य । प्रत्ययकारणं धूमज्ञानमभिजानस्य । प्राप्तिकारणं योगाङ्गानुष्ठानं विवेकख्यातेः ।

वियोगकारणं तदेवाशुद्धेः । अन्यत्वकारणं यथा सुवर्णस्य सुवर्णकारः । एवमेकस्य स्त्रीप्रत्ययस्याविद्या मूढत्वे द्वेषो दुःखत्वे

मिन्द्रियद्वारा वा स्वतॊ वा विषयस्य संक्रियाऽभिव्यक्तिस्तस्याः कारणं यथा रूपस्याऽऽलोकः । विकारकारणं मनसो विषयान्तरम् । यथा हि कण्डोः समाहितमनसो वल्लकीविपच्यमानपद्मस्वरश्रवणसमनन्तरमुन्मीलिताक्षस्य स्वरूपलावण्ययौवनसंपन्नाप्सरसं प्रलोभामिक्षमाणस्य समाधिमपहाय तस्यां सक्तं मनो बभूवेति । अत्रैव निदर्शनमाह — यथाऽग्निः पाकस्य तण्डुलादेः कठिनावयवसन्निवेशस्य प्रशैथिल्यववयवसंयोगलक्षणस्य विकारस्य कारणम् । सत एव विषयस्य प्रत्ययकारणं धूमज्ञानमभिजानस्येति । ज्ञायत इति ज्ञानमभिशासौ ज्ञानं चेत्यभिशातं तस्य । एतदुक्तं भवति — वर्तमानस्याभिज्ज्ञेयस्य प्रत्ययकारणतया कारणमिति । औत्सर्गिकनिरपेक्षाणां कारणानां कार्यक्रिया प्राप्तिस्तस्याः कुतश्चिदपवादोऽप्राप्तिः । यथा निम्नपसर्पणस्वभावानां प्रतिबन्धः सेतुना तथेहापि बुद्धिसत्त्वस्य सुखप्रकाशशीलस्य स्वाभाविकसुखविवेकस्यातिजनकता प्राप्तिः । सा कुतश्चिद्धर्मात्तमो वा प्रतिबन्धान्न भवति । धर्माद्योगाङ्गानुष्ठानाद्वा तदपनये तदप्रतिबद्धवृत्तिस्वभावत एव तज्जनकतया तदाप्नोति । यथा वक्ष्यति — निमित्तमप्रयोजकं प्रकृतीनां वरणभेदस्तु ततः क्षेत्रिकवदिति ।

तदेवं विवेकख्यातिलक्षणकार्यापेक्षया प्रातिकारणमुक्तम् । अवान्तरकार्यापेक्षया तु तदेव वियोगकारणमित्याह — वियोगकारणमिति । अन्यत्वकारणमाह — अन्यत्वकारणं यथा सुवर्णकारः सुवर्णस्य, कटककुण्डलकेयूरादिभ्यो भिन्नाभिन्नस्य भेदविवक्षया कटकादिभिन्नस्य सुवर्णस्य कुण्डलादन्यत्वम् । तथा च कटककारी सुवर्णकारः कुण्डलाद्भिन्नस्य सुवर्णस्यान्यत्वकुर्वन्नन्यत्वकारणम् । अग्निरपि पाकस्याऽन्यत्वकारणं यद्यपि तथाऽपि धर्मिणो धर्मयोः पुलाकत्वतण्डुलत्वयोर्भेदविवक्षया धर्मयोरुपजनापायेऽपि धर्म्यनुवर्तत इति न तस्यान्यत्वं शक्यं वक्तुमिति विकारमात्रकारणत्वमुक्तमिति न संकरः । न च संस्थानभेदो धर्मिणोऽन्यत्वकारणमिति व्याख्येयम् । सुवर्णकार इत्यस्यासंगतेः । बाह्यमन्यत्वकारणमुपनयस्याऽऽध्यात्मिकमुदाहरति — एवमेकस्येति । अविद्या कमनीयेयं कन्येत्यादिज्ञानम् । तन्मोहयोगात्स एव स्त्रीप्रत्ययो

Le livre VIII du *Speculum naturale* parle d'abord des matières minérales, partagées en quatre genres, savoir : corps fusibles ou métaux, pierres, matières sulfureuses, sels. Les pierres précieuses et minéraux proprement dits n'y sont pas décrits, étant réservés au livre IX.

L'histoire de chaque métal est présentée séparément, en suivant une marche systématique; le compilateur résume d'abord les textes anciens de Pline, d'Isidore de Séville et autres; puis vient pour chaque corps un chapitre alchimique : *De operatione auri in alchimia; De operatione argenti, cupri, stanni, plumbi, ferri, etc.*, chapitre où l'auteur reproduit des textes tirés de l'Alchimiste, des *Météorologiques* d'Aristote et de leur prétendue suite, de Rasès, d'Avicenne, etc., conformément à ce qui a été dit plus haut.

Aux chapitres LX et suivants commence l'étude des quatre esprits minéraux et du traitement (*operatio*) de chacun d'eux en alchimie.

Cela fait, l'auteur traite, au chapitre LXXIII, des autres minéraux, intermédiaires entre les corps et les esprits, et d'abord des aluns, des vitriols (*atramenta*), etc.

Il aborde ensuite la génération des minéraux, d'abord dans la nature, en exposant un mélange de chimères et d'observations réelles, tirées en grande partie des écrits latins d'Avicenne. Puis il examine leur génération artificielle, c'est-à-dire la pierre philosophale, ou élixir tinctorial, sous sa double forme : blanche pour l'argent, jaune (ou rouge) pour l'or. Suit une dissertation sur la réalité de l'alchimie, empruntée également au même auteur. L'indication des noms des principaux alchimistes (chap. LXXXVII) est prise également dans la traduction latine de l'ouvrage attribué à Avicenne.

Next once a year into Essex a hunting they go;
To see 'em pass along, O 'tis a most pretty shew:
Through Cheapside and Fenchurch-street, and so to Aldgate pump,
Each man with's spurs in's horses sides, and his back-sword cross his rump.

My lord he takes a staff in hand to beat the bushes o'er;
I must confess it was a work he ne'er had done before.
A creature bounceth from a bush, which made them all to laugh;
My lord he cried a hare a hare, but it prov'd an Essex calf.

And when they had done their sport, they came to London where they dwell,
Their faces all so torn and scratch'd, their wives scarce knew them well;
For 'twas a very great mercy, so many 'scap'd alive,
For of twenty saddles carried out, they brought again but five.

Privileges to hunt in certain districts, were frequently granted to individuals, either from favour, or as a reward for their services. Richard the first, gave to Henry de Grey, of Codnor, the manor of Turroe, in Essex, with permission to hunt the hare and the fox, in any lands belonging to the crown, excepting only the king's own desmean parks; and this special mark of the royal favour was confirmed by his brother John, when he succeeded to the throne.

Others obtained grants of land, on condition of their paying an annual tribute in horses, hawks, and hounds. And here I cannot help noticing a curious tenure, by which Bertram de Criol held the manor of Setene, or Seaton, in Kent, from Edward the first; he was to provide a man, called veltarius or huntsman, to lead three greyhounds when the king went into Gascony, so long as a pair of shoes, valued at fourpence, should last him.

68. بسيلة (بسباة) cod. Hamb. Cicerculae genus.
Alba, multis granis plena; optima Kahirensis. Cf.. al. loc.

69. بستيناج Bastinâch. Tribulus. Aegyptiis est خلال, gingidii species, visnaga. Seminum decoctio odontalgiae opponitur. Cf. حسك hasak.

70. بشام Bashâm. Arbor balsamifera.
Abu Hanifa: Arbor foliolis parvis, saturejae etiam minoribus, fructu destituta, succi lactei plena, bene olens. In montibus. Foliis nigrescunt capilli. Elnabati: Frequens in montibus prope Meccam, flore ex albo flavo, fructibus racemosis, edulibus. Invenitur et in Hispania. Lignum vocatur lignum balsamicum. Qui hanc arborem fructibus carere dicunt, falluntur. — Spreng. hist. rei herb. p. 257. Amyris Opobalsamum. Forsk. Fl. Aeg. p. 79. Ab. dallat. p. 93. 94.

71. بشنة Bishna. Milii genus.
Elgafeki: Planta parva, multicaulis, quae super saxa sese extendit; foliis succo viscoso, melligeno madidis; flore minutissimo, albo; seminibus parvis amaris, stypticis. — Galium viscosum sive Aparine?

A Deus, aitque omnia posse ab eo, qui ligauit, dissolui. Rursus audis in libris de Legibus
cœlum, astraque Deos, quin ipsum Solem iuxta ea, quæ Mercurius prior, maximum
Deum esse. Hæc igitur eo modo interpretaberis, quo Trismegistus totius Philoso-
phiæ princeps, præcipue Platonicę, docuit. Nec opus est confutationibus, cui ipsimet
seipsos declarēt, auguste fatentes, ac sancte Deum, Bonumque, æternum, conditorem omnium, unicum,
singulareque, imparticabile, Bonitatis ineffabilis, cætera facticia, et uel noie tantum, uel
simulata quanda, et honore affecta Bonitate uel Diuinitate. Eodem sensu oportebit in-
telligere Aristotele: quandoquidem omnis apud eum Theologia, a maioribus Græcis, et
Barbaris manauit. Vt cœli Diuinitate, necessario se loco habeat, quo habuere, a quis
bus ipse didicit, retines sibi uera pietate, uerioremque Diuinitate, a qua Diuinitas ue-
nerit cœli, eo quo barbari docuere modo, non in æternum pendes, generataque, sed facta
a magna Bonitate, ac Diuinitate, rerum cæterarum creatrice, cuius sit tanta magnitudo,
ut sola potuerit, sola meruerit esse sempiterna. Cætera quonia distant in immensum ab
ea, noua Diuinitate, Bonitateque fuisse donata. Hæc Aristoteles certe fateri cogetur, et
quide concessus est, siue illu huc rapiente natura, siue animo suo ueriora cernete, respi-
ciente ad eos, a quibus manabat ea, quæ scribebat ipse. Eiusde etia alibi confessus est
Trismegistus tanta esse, tam differente ab omnibus maiestate, ut dicat potentiæ eius
<greek>ὅτε τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, ὅτε τὰ θεῖα προβάλλει ἅμ τις μηδέποτε ᾄδῃ κἀντῶ, μηδὲ ᾄνω ὁμοιοῦντι ἡ γύσω τῷ θεῷ. ὅθεν ὅμοιον τῷ ἀνομοίῳ τὸ μόνον, ᾧ ἑνί</greek>, Nec humana, nec diuina esse comparanda.
Nec quæ deorsum, nec quæ sursum Deo similia arbitreris. Nihil simile dissimili,
et soli, et uni. Ex quibus probant ea, quæ nostra Theologia clamat: Vnu eum esse sem-
piternum, uere immortale, omnibus dissimile: factos aut eo Deos, et homines, quos
nia ille solus debet esse sempiternus. Hæc eade, de Bonitate item diuine in
B Protagora Plato. Quo libro ex sententia Simonidis asserit, hoiem bonum inueniri per-
difficile esse: fieri aut posse, ut ad aliquod tempus. Sed cum bonus fuerit, perseuerare in
bonitatis habitu, uirtuque bonum esse, ut dixit Pittacus, impossibile esse, minimeque hu-
manu. Sed solu Deum hoc honore preditu esse, homine aut fieri no posse, qn sit malus.

Deum creatorem omnium rerum dicere Platonem. Testimonia, quibus appa-
ret eum Vniuersi conditorem nuncupasse. Prolem diuinam autorem mun-
di esse Platoni, cui det Patrem in Epistola.

Hic dicit quod Porphirius tradidit noticiam quinque uniuersalium. que sunt genus species differentia proprium et accidens. quorum noticia utilis est ad habendum predicamentorum noticiam. ut patet in principio sui libri. si ne quorum uniuersalium cognitione nihil potest sciri in logica. hec autem uniuersalia secundum Platonis doctrinam sunt monstra. quia deficiunt a suis perfectionibus. quia per ipsum sunt per se subsistentia. et ita non possunt singularibus dare esse nomen et rationem. quod tamen secundum veritatem eis conuenit secundum diffinitionem uniuersalis. qua dicit Uniuersale est unum in multis. scilicet singularibus seu inferioribus.

Hic dicit quod Porphirius tradidit noticiam quinque uniuersalium. que sunt genus species differentia proprium et accidens. quorum noticia utilis est ad habendum predicamentorum noticiam. ut patet in principio sui libri. si ne quorum uniuersalium cognitione nihil potest sciri in logica. hec autem uniuersalia secundum Platonis doctrina sunt monstra. quia deficiunt a suis perfectionibus. quia per ipsum sunt per se subsistentia. et ita non possunt singularibus dare esse nomen et rationem. quod tamen secundum veritate eis conuenit secundum diffinitionem uniuersalis. qua dicit Uniuersale est unum pluribus in multis. scilicet singularibus seu inferioribus.

<margin>Indien die twee Vasalle Steeden van een Primier Noble in Zeeland de-pendent blijven, foo is Holland niet alleen door fituatie maar ook door intereft van Regee-ring, by na gansch van Zeeland af-gefcheiden.</margin>
vrugtbaare, volkrijke, door magtige Zee-stroomen van alle haare Gebuuren afgescheidene Eylanden: en dat het daar en booven verscheide Steeden en Sterkten, leggende op den bodem des Generaliteits, in Vlaanderen en Braband, in zijn geweld heeft weeten te bekomen; alsoo de Heeren van Zeeland, in Lillo, Liefkenshoek, Axel, ter Neuse en Biervliet, de commandementen vergeeven ende de Garnisoenen verleggen. Sulks Zeeland sig selven schijnd teegen alle fijne Gebuuren, met fijne eige kragten, feer wel te sullen konnen beschermen: ende dat daar en booven de twee goede Zee-haavens in Walcheren, Vlissingen en Veere, seer wel leggen om de Hollandsche Negotie naar de West, met haare Zee-rooveryen te bekommeren.

Quid? cum in Prologo libri III. fastidiose se in coetum recipi queritur, & in prologo libri V. Particulonem dicat
> *nomen chartis victurum suis,*
> *Latinis dum manebit pretium litteris.*

ex tacitis amicorum laudibus hanc gloriae immortalitatem eum sperasse putamus, an publicis virorum eruditissimorum suffragiis? Et fane cum coetum nominat, utique eum definit, quem Romae fuisse accepimus eorum virorum, quorum scripta Criticorum calculis probata erant. Porro qui illa conveniunt, nisi omnium manibus versatos hos Phaedri libellos existimamus, ex Prologo libri III.
> *Suspicione siquis errabit sua*
> *Et rapiet ad se, quod erit commune omnium,*
> *Stulte nudabit animi conscientiam.*
> *Huic excusatum me velim nihilo minus.*
> *Neque enim notare singulos mens est mihi,*
> *Verum ipsam vitam & mores hominum ostendere.*

Piget plura proferre, nullus enim Prologus est, epilogus nullus in fine librorum, quin editas publice a se fabellas doceat. Miror autem qui diverse a nobis sentiunt, in eam opinionem esse adductos, quod Sejani metum ostendit Phaedrus in prologo libri III. quasi ipse AElius Sejanus hoc nomine, ac non potius homo, moribus ejus non dissimilis intelligatur. Nam si ipsum Sejanum intelligas, qui, quaeso, ausus est homo libertinus eum, sub saevissimo Principe crudeliter dominantem, tam acerbe perstringere in carmine publico? publicum enim fuisse ex iis perspicimus, quae modo ex hoc Prologo delibavimus. Aut si ausus hoc est Phaedrus vitae suae prodigus, qui, quaeso, factum, ut tantam linguae licentiam impunitam tulerit? tulisse autem videtur, quod interposito tempore reliqui fabularum libri prodierunt. μαρτυριῶν δίκη, εἰσήκει· ἐν δὲ τῷ δικαστηρίῳ πάντα μὲν ἡμῶν εἰπόντων ἃ πρῶτον, πολ-

τι μὴ συναχθῆναι, ἀλλὰ συγχέαι τὰς ψήφους, ἀφίστατο μὲν δικαιογένης τοῖν δυοῖν
μορίοιν τοῦ κλήρου, τοῖς δικαιογένους ἀδελφαῖς· καὶ ὡμολόγει ἀναμφισβήτητα τὴν λύ-
σειν ἡμῶν ταῦτα τὰ μόρια. καὶ ταῦτ’ ἐπύθετο αὐτῷ Λεωχάρης οὗτος, καὶ ὡμολόγει· φή-
σειν οὐ μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ μισθόλεμος ὁ πωλητής, καὶ τοῦ του ὑμῖν τοὺς μάρτυρας
παρέξομαι. μάρτυρες. ἡμεῖς τοίνυν ταῦτα παισθέντες ὑπὸ Λεωχάρης·

I, al. 2, sequentia tradit, inquiens, Miraculum fecit Deus dum creauit patrem nostrum Adamum, et formauit eum ex quatuor elementis, miscuit elementa, ita tamen ut non discordarent inter se. Primum cum secundo, et tertium cum quarto miscuit, humidum cum arido et calidum cum frigido, inuisibile cum uisibili, palpabile cum impalpabili, (quasi uero haec misceri possent, quod materiae tantum est proprium,) Duo fecit ex palpabili, et duo ex impalpabili, tria fecit ex arido, et unum ex humido, Tria fecit ex frigido, et unum ex calido. Nouerat Architectus, ubi constituendum esset penetrale, et fundauit angulos domus in quatuor Elementis. ༄༅། །ཆུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་ལ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཡིན། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །མཐའ་ཡས་པ་དབས་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཐོག་མ་དང་ཐ་མ་མེད་པའི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། །གསོལ་ལོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་གི་ཆུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་ལ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །གསོལ་ལོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་གི་ཆུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་ལ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །མཐའ་ཡས་པ་དབས་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཐོག་མ་དང་ཐ་མ་མེད་པའི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། །གསོལ་ལོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་གི་ཆུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་ལ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཡིན། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །གསོལ་ལོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་གི་ཆུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་ལ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །

malus exiet. Et aperit cerebrum quod est obstructum et clarificat ipsum cerebrum. Et expellit malos humores et humiditates ex quibus veniunt vomiti. Et ventus malos et malum sanguinem ac sudores expellit. Et ex illa lotione veniunt in sompno que venturi sunt.

Ad liberandum oculos ex palpebratos.
Recipe unum ciatum de meliori vino quod poteris habere si esset maluasia melius esset et sit vinum album. Tunc recipe quartum unius uncie de tucia alexandrina et extingue dictam tuciam in dicto vino ad minimum decem vicibus et permitte residere per horam. Tunc euacua clarum ad unum aliud vitrum. Tunc recipe dictam tuciam videis quartam partem et tere eam minutissime et pone in dicto vino et cum illo infirmus lavet sibi oculos sepe. Et si non liberabit hoc. Recipe modicum de felle unius porci et ipone dicto vino et similiter lavet se sepe ut supra. Et ad huc si hoc non recedet illa rubedo. tunc recipe albuginem unius oui et pone ad unam scutellam peutiens eam bene ita quod fiat clara sicut aqua Et non bene quod infirmus deponat se super lectum extensus per tres horas ad minimum: Balneando primo oculos cum aqua supradicta vel vino. Tunc habeat unum pannum lineum vel stopam et madider in albugine oui et super ponat oculis et sic iaceat per tres horas. Tunc resurgat et vadat sic per camera sepe balneando sibi oculos cum dicto vino Et sic faciat per tres vel quatuor dies vel plus. et sine fallo liberabitur.

Ad pussione oculi si supueniat aliqua nebula propter pussione vel homini vel equo. Recipe de succo edere et modicum de optima maluasia distempa insimul et cum penna pone in oculum bis in die et statim liberabit.

Ad facienda ceram argentea pro sigillis.
Accipe unam partem cere et duas mercurii et calefac ad ignem digitis conterendo donec eque totaliter sit inceratu et mortificatu. Et postea ipsam ceram calefactam sigillabis.

<header>DU MONDE PRIMITIF.</header>
<sig>M</sig>

Nous pourrons également aller beaucoup plus loin par le rétablissement de la Langue & des Connoissances primitives, & par l'ensemble de nos recherches.

Les Livres sacrés des Hébreux ne feront pas les seuls sur lesquels nous répandrons de la lumiere par notre marche. Il en sera à peu-près de même de la plupart des Livres anciens, sur-tout de ceux que nous avons indiqués dans l'article des Cosmogonies & des Théogonies comparées.

Nous ferons en état, par exemple, de donner une Traduction de l'EDDA, de cette Mythologie des Enfans du Nord, écrite en vieux Runique, plus claire que celles que l'on nous en a données en diverses Langues, & de l'accompagner d'un Glossaire qui expliquera nombre de ces mots allégoriques qu'on n'avoit pu entendre, & qui présentera les raports frapans de la Langue dans laquelle l'EDDA fut écrit avec les autres Langues, comme nous aurons fait voir les raports de cette Mythologie avec celles des autres Peuples.

Un grand nombre d'endroits des Poésies d'ORPHÉE, d'HÉSIODE, d'HOMERE, &c. & des anciens Historiens, deviendront plus aisés à traduire, plus clairs, plus intéressans par-là même.

II. L'on ne sera donc pas étonné qu'une portion considérable de ces Miscellanea soit composée d'OBSERVATIONS CRITIQUES que nous aurons eu occasion de faire dans le cours de ces recherches pour rectifier des méprises jusques ici inévitables ; & que ces observations donnent lieu à des discussions curieuses & intéressantes.

III. Enfin, ces recherches se terminent par un grand nombre de Morceaux ou DISSERTATIONS sur des points d'Histoire, de Chronologie, de Philosophie ancienne, &c. liés avec tous les objets précédens, trop étendus pour faire corps avec eux ; & trop intéressans pour être négligés.

Tambien podriamos añedir por vltima causa, el aspero y riguroso frio, que á las tiernas y delicadas hojas, flores, y retoños, suele quemar y abrassar (como dize el vulgo) y esto haze apagando el calor natural con que vive y se conserva la dicha hoja y planta. Todo lo qual supuesto, es facil satisfacer alo que enel problema se pregunta, y assi respondiendo por orden digo, que los arboles desta tierra jamas pierden la hoja, por quanto causa ninguna delas que arriba deziamos, es bastante á secarla, y hazerla caer: primeramente no pueden caerse en tiempo de hivierno, porque como estamos y bivimos dentro dela torridazona, apartase el sol muy poco de nosotros por tiempo de hivierno, y assi no podemos al tal tiempo llamar hivierno, sino vn perpetuo verano, pues siempre anda el sol cerca de nosotros mayormente que como estos arboles dela tierra se crian siempre en tierras calientes jamas les desampara el calor, que es el que vivifica, y conserva la planta: menos se deshojan y secan los arboles indianos, por falta de humedad, porque en verano sobra la humedad delas lluvias, y en hivierno la que desciende, y baxa de las sierras á regar las dichas tierras calientes, donde avemos dicho criarse los frutales de indias. Pues el ardiente calor del estio, menos puede secar las hojas delos arboles, porque como en estio son las aguas, la humedad dellas embota y refrena la gran fuerza de calor, y assi podemos con verdad dezir, que en la primavera reyna mas calor en indias, que por estio, á causa de que las lluvias que tiemplan el calor del estio, no han aun comenzado por la primavera: pues frio grandissimo que abrase las hojas de los arboles, jamas tal se vio en tierras muy calientes de indias, y ansi por todas las sobredichas causas no pierden los arboles dela tierra la hoja en ningun tiempo: ayudando á todo lo dicho el ser los arboles de la tierra salvages, y agrestes, y por el consiguiente rezios y muy duros, y assi resisten con fuerza á todo contrario de frio y calor, los quales como he dicho, no son muy fuertes en las tierras calientes de indias.

Y si me dixessen que como el capuli, y el manzanillo llammado xocote, siendo arboles de indias pierden la hoja, respondo que estos dos arboles antes son de España que delas indias, pues el xocote es derechamente specie de mispero, y el capuli specie de cerezo.

22½. The length of a longish quadrilateral is 120 (*dandas*) and the breadth is 40. The ditch around is as big as 4 *dandas* in breadth and 3 in depth. (Find out the cubical contents.)

The rule for arriving at the value of the cubical contents of an excavation, when the depth of the excavation varies (at various points), and also for arriving, when the cubical contents of an excavation are known, at the depth of digging necessary in the case of another (known) area (so that the cubical contents may be the same):—

23½. The sum of the depths (measured in different places) is divided by the number of places; this gives rise to the (average) depth. This multiplied by the top area (of the excavation) gives rise to the (required) cubical contents of the excavation in the case where that area is trilateral, quadrilateral or circular. The cubical contents (of a given excavation), when divided by the (known) value of another area, gives rise to the depth (to which there should be digging, so that the resulting cubical contents may be the same).

*Examples in illustration thereof.*

But that which is useless to them, and beneficial to us, will be the reward which we receive from them [of our attention to their concerns]. In sacrifices, therefore, we should abstain from animals. For, though all things are in reality the property of the Gods, yet plants appear to be our property; since we sow and cultivate them, and nourish them by other attentions which we pay to them. We ought to sacrifice, therefore, from our own property, and not from the property of others; since that which may be procured at a small expense, and which may easily be obtained, is more holy, more acceptable to the Gods, and better adapted to the purposes of sacrifice, and to the exercise of continual piety. Hence, that which is neither holy, nor to be obtained at a small expense, is not to be offered in sacrifice, even though it should be present.

14. But that animals do not rank among things which may be procured easily, and at a small expense, may be seen by directing our view to the greater part of our race: for we are not now to consider that some men abound in sheep, and others in oxen. In the first place, therefore, there are many nations that do not possess any of those animals which are offered in sacrifice, some ignoble animals, perhaps, excepted. And, in the second place, most of those that dwell in cities themselves, possess these but rarely. But if some one should say that the inhabitants of cities have not mild fruits in abundance; yet, though this should be admitted, they are not in want of the other vegetable productions of the earth; nor is it so difficult to procure fruits as it is to procure animals. Hence an abundance of fruits, and other vegetables, is more easily obtained than that of animals. But which is obtained with facility, and at a small expense, contributes to incessant and universal piety.

*Hamzah's Precepts:*—The first precept of Hamzah enjoins veracity in speech; the second, protection and mutual aid to the brethren in faith; the third, renunciation of all forms of former worship and false belief; the fourth, repudiation of the devil (*Iblīs*) and all forces of evil; the fifth, confession of the unity of the Ḥākim-God; the sixth, acquiescence in his acts no matter what they be; and the seventh, absolute submission and resignation to his divine will in both secret and public.¹

*Sources and Operation:*—The first two precepts enunciated by the founder of Druzism are ethical in their nature and therefore difficult to trace back to their origin. The genealogy of the third and fourth is likewise difficult to ascertain. The fifth is the dogma we treated before, and the rest are corollaries from that dogma. The operation of the first precept is, of course, circumscribed by the already established law of dissimulation.

Of these principles the second has perhaps been the most potent force in the life and history of the Druze people. It has made of the Druze community one compact social body, presenting more the aspects of a religious fraternal order than a sect. This fraternal feature is one of the distinctive characteristics of the Druze people and has, in a large measure, contributed to their survival to the present day. It has enabled them at the time of crisis to act in unison and as one body moved primarily by motives of self-interest and by the instinct of self-preservation.

---

¹ These precepts occur in most of their leading religious tracts.

ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཚེ། །གསལ་མཁས་པས་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཚེ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མི་མཐོང་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །ཚེས་གཅིག་གིས་ལས་གསལ་བཞིན་དུ་མི་སྤྱོད་དོ། །བཟོད་པར་བྱ། །བཟོད་པར་དང༌། །བཟོད་པར་དཔལ་ཡར་མི་མིམས། །ཚེས་གཅིག་གིས་ལས་གསལ་བཞིན་དུ་མི་སྤྱོད་དོ། །དེ་ཚེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཚེ། །ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་གཟུགས་མེད་པར་གསལ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །དེ་ལས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཚེ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །ཚེས་གཅིག་གིས་ལས་གསལ་བཞིན་དུ་མི་སྤྱོད་དོ། །དེ་ཚེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཚེ། །གསལ་

->Dertiende Tafereel.<-

**Z**Ie hoe de Chriftenen in ftilte hier gezeten,
Aandachtig luisteren, naar 't levendmaakend woord,
Dat als een snydend zwaerd het harde hart doorboort,
Of brandt gelyk een vuur, tot zuiv'ring van 't geweeten.

Deez' strekt de schrift tot troost in zyne tegenspoed,
Dien sterkt zy in de deugd, door onvervalschte leering,
Een ander wekt zy op tot boete en zielsbeekeering,
Of ondersteunt met kracht het wankelend gemoed.

Dus strekt zy deez' tot melk, en dien tot vaste spyze,
Dat hen van tyd tot tyd in 't rein geloof versterkt,
Waardoor de Chriften ziel haar overtreeding merkt,
En stof vindt dat zy Godt voor zyn genade pryze.

Dank, Chriften, uwen Heer voor 't dierbaar heilkleinood,
Veel krachtiger van glans dan Aarons borstgesteente,
De zuivere Urim en de Thummim der gemeente,
De zon, waar voor 't gesternte der oude wet verschoot.

CCXXXV. — HIERACI DIACONO.
*Non videmus manticam in tergo.* Adagium. Persius sat. 4. *Phaedrus: Peras imposuit nobis duas, etc.*

Decipis forsan teipsum putans te cernere quod in rem sit tuam. Cernere quidem vidéris, non cérnis tamen, sed plerumque in tuis rebus caecutis. Si enim quod ambiguum incertumque putatur, honorificum opinaris, neque mihi, neque tibi judicium permittas, sed communicans cum judicio prudentiaque praestantibus, sententiam ab illis mutuare.

CCXXXVI. — JACOBO LECTORI.
*Malos esse fugiendos. Consuetudo enim altera natura.*

Fuge, o charissime, improbos: quippe noxium quemdam habitum animae usu et consuetudine suasim ingenerant. Plerumque enim fallentes seipsos quasi optimi sint et fortissimi, quasique tales casus laedere non possint, clam in mala se lenteque velut in barathrum praecipitant. Consuetudo enim quid magnum, et in naturam paulatim abit; alteramque esse naturam quidam affirmant. Alii etiam a consuetudine superari naturam, illud veteris poetae adhibentes, asserunt.

*Gutta cavum reddit saxum, dum decidit usque.*
*Et vero quid saxo durius? quid aqua mollius?*
*attamen ictu assiduo naturae vincitur durities.*

CCXXXVII. — HIERACI DIACONO.
*Temperantia sanitatis mater.* (Vide epist. 63, 148, 158.)

Siquidem valetudinem corporis curas, sufficienti tibi copia contentus esto. Haec enim illam parit. Si vero per delicias illud turgescere ac lascivire cupis, falleris: non modo armando ipsum adversus animam atque infrene reddens, sed et radicem ac fontem immedicabilium reddens morborum.

CCXXXVIII. — THEODORO SCHOLASTICO.

ΣΑΕ. — ΙΕΡΑΚΙ ΔΙΑΚΟΝΩ.

Αὐτὸς μὲν ἴσως σεαυτὸν ἀπατᾷς, ὡς ὁρῶν τὸ σαυτοῦ συμφέρον· ἐγὼ δὲ φαίην, ὅτι δοκεῖς μὲν ὁρᾶν, ὁρᾷς δὲ οὐδαμῶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ κομιδῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τυφλώττεις. Εἰ δὲ ἀμφίδοξόν σοι εἶναι δοκεῖ τὸ ἔνδοξον, μήτε ἐμοί, μήτε σεαυτῷ τὴν κρίσιν ἐπιτρέψῃς· ἀλλὰ ἀνακοινωσάμενος τοῖς συνέσει διαφέρουσι, παρ’ αὐτῶν δέχου τὴν ψῆφον.

Φεῦγε, ὦ φίλτατε, τοὺς πονηρούς, ἄτε λυμικήν τινα κατάστασιν τῇ ψυχῇ λανθανόντως διὰ τῆς συνηθείας κατασκευάζοντας· πολλοὶ γὰρ ἀπατήσαντες ἑαυτοὺς ὡς ἄριστοι καὶ κράτιστοι, καὶ ὑπὸ τοιούτων συντυχιοῶν μὴ καταβλαπτόμενοι, ἔλαβον εἰς τὰ αὐτὰ ἐκείνοις ἠρέμα καὶ κατὰ μικρὸν κατενεχθέντες βάραθρα. Decipis forsan teipsum putans te cernere quod in rem sit tuam. Cernere quidem vidēris, non cernis tamen, sed plerumque in tuis rebus caecutis. Si enim quod ambiguum incertumque putatur, honorificum opinaris, neque mihi, neque tibi judicium permittas, sed communicans cum judicio prudentiaque praestantibus, sententiam ab illis mutuare.

CCXXXVI. — JACOBO LECTORI.
*Malos esse fugiendos. Consuetudo enim altera natura.*

Fuge, o charissime, improbos: quippe noxium quemdam habitum animae usu et consuetudine suasim ingenerant. Plerique enim fallentes seipsos quasi optimi sint et fortissimi, quasique tales casus laedere non possint, clam in mala se lenteque velut in barathrum praecipitant. Consuetudo enim quid magnum, et in naturam paulatim abit; alteramque esse naturam quidam affirmant. Alii etiam a consuetudine superari naturam, illud veteris poetae adhibentes, asserunt.

*Gutta cavum reddit saxum, dum decidit usque.*
*Et vero quid saxo durius? quid aqua mollius? attamen ictu assiduo naturae vincitur durities.*

Nuperrime autem G. Koertius de ea parte Cynegetici quae technica dicitur lucubrationem instituit, quam priusquam ad finem perduxisset morte est interceptus. Primum exposuit non modo dispositionem incommodam esse, sed ipsam doctrinam adeo mancam et obscuram ut venatoribus vix utilis esse posset. Et id quidem iure eum contendisse fatendum est: sed confirmat coniecturam nostram de huiusce libelli origine. Xenophontis enim heres, homo studiorum certe rhetoricorum haud rudis, sed in scribendo parum habilis, rerum seriem, sicut in volumine sibi tradito perscriptam invenerat, integram servavit nec regulis ex sua scientia addere quidquam ausus est quod illustraret aut in ordinem idoneum redigeret.

At multa, inquit Koertius, in hac parte operis ita falsa sunt praecepta ut nullo modo a viro vere venandi perito conscripta esse potuerint. Quam sententiam quominus pleno exemplorum numero exponeret et stabiliret fatis est prohibitus. Sed nonnulla saltem quae vituperavit aut vituperaturus erat controversa potius quam falsa esse dixerim. Suadet enim Cynegetici scriptor ut leporem, ubi a catulis captus sit, iis discerpendum tradat venator. Quod consilium reprehendit Koertius tamquam plane absurdum. At id ipsum commendat Blanius, vir haud minus quam Koertius artis venatoriae gnarus. Quid? In libro de Re Equestri Simonem laudat Xenophon quod pedum bonitatem in equo sonitu prodi docuerit: id quod perspicue falsam esse declarant Bourgelatus et Berenger. Man bemerkt dies auch sowohl auf der Violine wie auf dem Cello deutlich, wenigstens für den tiefsten Eigenton, wenn man die entsprechenden Noten auf den Saiten hervorbringt. Sie klingen besonders voll, und der Grundton dieser Klänge tritt besonders stark heraus. In schwächerem Grade meine ich dasselbe auch für das a' der Violine, welches ihrem höheren Eigentone entspricht, gehört zu haben.

Da der tiefste Ton der Violine g ist, so können von den Obertönen ihrer Klänge nur die höheren Octaven ihrer drei tiefsten Noten durch die Resonanz des höheren Eigentons ihres Luftraumes etwas verstärkt werden, im Allgemeinen müssen dagegen die Grundtöne, namentlich ihrer höheren Noten, den Obertönen gegenüber begünstigt werden, weil die genannten Grundtöne den eigenen Tönen der Luftmasse näher liegen als die Obertöne. Es wird dadurch eine ähnliche Wirkung wie am Claviere hervorgebracht, wo ebenfalls durch die Construction der Hämmer die Obertöne der tiefen Noten begünstigt, die der höheren geschwächt sind. Beim Cello, dessen tiefste Saite C giebt, liegt der stärkere Eigenton der Luftmasse ebenso wie bei der Violine, eine Quarte bis Quinte höher als der der tiefsten Saite. Es entsteht dadurch ein ähnliches Verhältniss der begünstigten und nicht begünstigten Töne, aber alles eine Duodecime tiefer. Bei der Bratsche dagegen liegen die am meisten begünstigten Töne, etwa dem h' entsprechend, nicht zwischen denen der ersten und zweiten Saite, sondern zwischen der zweiten und dritten, was mit der veränderten Klangfarbe dieses Instruments zusammenzuhängen scheint. In Ziffern lässt sich dieser Einfluss leider noch nicht ausdrücken. Sehr stark ist das Maximum der Resonanz für die eigenen Töne der Luftmasse nicht gerade ausgesprochen; es würde auch sonst eine viel grössere Ungleichartigkeit in der Tonleiter der genannten Streichinstrumente hervorrufen, sobald man den Theil der Scala passirte, in welchem die eigenen Töne ihrer Luftmassen liegen. Demgemäss ist zu vermuthen, dass auch der Einfluss auf die relative Stärke der einzelnen Partialtöne der Klänge dieser Instrumente nicht sehr hervortretend ist.

Mercury digested two times its weight with mica, is capable of 'killing' the eight metals. It (juice of *khecarī*) can calcine sulphur, orpiment and gold. It also 'fixes' mercury. All metals on being calcined with this, lose their 'essences' (*sattva*). 127-128

It (juice of *khecarī*) can also calcine coral, liquefy mica, and 'kill' diamond. There is no doubt about that. 129

<margin>Killing of mercury (vss. 130 131).</margin> O Beautiful-faced! I shall now tell another means by which the *Sādhaka* (performer) attains *siddhi*. Mercury and the juice of *harindarī* kept in the hole of the cow's horn, is to be deposited in heaps of paddy. 130-131 (line 1)

<margin>Increase of transmutation power of mercury (vss. 131-133).</margin> O God-praised! mercury, which is 'killed' with the juice of this plant being digested with equal weight of gold, can attain the power of transmuting ten hundred thousand times its weight of base metals into noble metals. If digested (with gold) four times of its own weight, it (mercury) is endowed with the capacity of transforming hundred million times its weight of base metals into noble metals. When digested with (gold) six times of its own weight, it (mercury) acquires the capacity of transmuting base metals into noble metals by its 'touch' only. 131 (line 2)-132

When digested seven times its weight with gold, it (mercury) can reach the stage of transmuting base metals into noble metals by its 'smoke'. Thus digested eight times its weight with gold, the transmutation is performed by the 'sight' of mercury only (*avalokita*). 133 (line 1)

One, having no knowledge of the *kulauṣadhīs*, moves in a bewildered state. 133 (line 2)

<margin>Kulauṣadhīs and tṛṇauṣadhīs (vss. 133-135).</margin> With the juice of *tṛṇauṣadhī* nothing can be achieved (in the pursuit of alchemical preparations). Hence the knowledge of *kulauṣadhī* is to be attained with great care. 134

There are sixty-four groups of *divyauṣadhī* plants. The foolish and the one allured by the illusion of Śiva, are not acquainted with them. 135

<margin>Inefficacy of tṛṇauṣadhīs in mercurial operations (vss. 136-138).</margin> The *tṛṇauṣadhīs* are not heavenly (*adivya*, i.e. non-medicinal plant). They grow in the hollow of caves. Mercury is never 'fixed' with the juice of *tṛṇauṣadhī*. 136

<column-break/>

O Beautiful lady! mercury, treated with the juice of *tṛṇauṣadhī*, undergoes no loss of weight, i.e. elimination of its impurities (*akṣaya*). It cannot endure the heat of fire. The gold (produced from base metals) on being treated with this mercury can never stand equal to gold (either natural or perfectly transmuted gold) in matter of leaves (i.e. constituting layers), in roasting (i.e. showing unusual colour when) cutting into two. 137

The gold, yielded as a result of the treatment of any metal with mercury thus prepared with the juice of this plant, can reach a stage, which is up to the half way level as attained in the case of a total (perfect) conversion. O my dear wife! as it is not perfectly 'fixed' the gold prepared from it should never be used for the attainment of *dharma, artha, kāma* and *mokṣa*. 138

Devī asked :

How mercury being 'killed', gives life to others? How lifeless plant enlivens mercury which has been 'killed'? 139

<margin>Efficacy of kulauṣadhīs in mercurial operations (vss. 139-142).</margin> Śiva said:

O Pārvatī! mercury when 'swooned' (*mūrchita*) by the application of medicinal plant (*divyauṣadhī*) becomes devoid of its *kālikā* impurity, and is enlivened. 140

This mercury, being free from impurities, also removes the impurities of others. By the application of this (mercury), all metals become devoid of their impurities. 141

Who can say the perfectly 'swooned' mercury as 'killed'? Mercury loses its own existence by the application of juice of medicinal plants. 142

O Goddess! I shall now tell another plant for the 'fixation' of mercury. Diamond is to be 'killed' with the aid of *kṣamāpālana*; likewise gold is to be 'killed' with this. 143

<margin>Power of mercury that has been 'killed' with the aid of diamond and gold calces (vss. 143-147).</margin> The ashes of diamond and gold are to be tied perfectly (i.e. mixed together). This (compound) product, on being calcined with the juice of *niśācara*, is to be calcined with mercury (*narajīva*). 144

Mercury thus calcined with the aid of this calx becomes 'killed'. This mercury is to undergo quick-exhaustion with the aid of this plant-substance. With this mercury, taken with the juice of *niśācara*, one is blessed with the strength like that of Śiva. 145

O my dear wife! as it is not perfectly 'fixed' the gold prepared from it should never be used for the attainment of *dharma, artha, kāma* and *mokṣa*. 138

Devī asked :

How mercury being 'killed', gives life to others? How lifeless plant enlivens mercury which has been 'killed'? 139

<margin>Efficacy of kulauṣadhīs in mercurial operations (vss. 139-142).</margin> Śiva said:

O Pārvatī! mercury when 'swooned' (*mūrchita*) by the application of medicinal plant (*divyauṣadhī*) becomes devoid of its *kālikā* impurity, and is enlivened. 140

This mercury, being free from impurities, also removes the impurities of others. By the application of this (mercury), all metals become devoid of their impurities. 141

Who can say the perfectly 'swooned' mercury as 'killed'? Mercury loses its own existence by the application of juice of medicinal plants. 142

O Goddess! I shall now tell another plant for the 'fixation' of mercury. Diamond is to be 'killed' with the aid of *kṣamāpālana*; likewise gold is to be 'killed' with this. 143

<margin>Power of mercury that has been 'killed' with the aid of diamond and gold calces (vss. 143-147).</margin> The ashes of diamond and gold are to be tied perfectly (i.e. mixed together). This (compound) product, on being calcined with the juice of *niśācara*, is to be calcined with mercury (*narajīva*). 144

Mercury thus calcined with the aid of this calx becomes 'killed'. This mercury is to undergo quick-exhaustion with the aid of this plant-substance. With this mercury, taken with the juice of *niśācara*, one is blessed with the strength like that of Śiva. 145

The liberal mind naturally experiences a difficulty in disbelieving where, a possibility being granted, the testimony in support of a matter is fair and honourable. And though sensible evidence and more than this sometimes is required to silence negative assertion; yet reason, supported by her witnesses, may enervate it, and induce that strict investigation and thought which should always precede experiment, but which the multitude have never yet been found willing to undertake; and are consequently led astray in progress, and learn as it were by chance. It is said that Lord Bacon instituted certain experiments with a view to the discovery of the philosopher's stone, and in the *Advancement of Learning* he faithfully recognises the possibility, as does also Sir Isaac Newton in his works; while Leibnitz devoted his early life to the pursuit: nor did either of these great men, though they were practically unsuccessful themselves, condemn the ancient tradition or deny its validity. Yet it would seem to be more ordinarily natural to the human mind to reject those things, which it has neither been early imbued in the belief of, nor instructed to understand; besides individual research into mere possibilities, and because facts only are alleged, is too hopeless and arduous for this short life, which requires a definite assurance of success, and fruit even from the smallest labour.
